inhibitor

/in-HIB-ih-ter/ - the stress falls on HIB · noun

Hear It

What It Means

Inhibitor means a substance or influence that slows or blocks a process — in science writing, the agent that binds part of the machinery so a reaction cannot run.

The pipeline owes its forty-year life to a corrosion inhibitor, a film of molecules that coats the steel and starves the rust of any purchase.

Example

The lab's best blood-pressure drug does nothing to the heart at all. It is an inhibitor: its molecules fit into an enzyme's working slot the way a bent key fits a lock — snugly, and uselessly — so the enzyme can no longer produce the hormone that tightens blood vessels. The vessels relax because a single step upstream has been quietly jammed.

Inhibitor is the precise word because the drug neither destroys the enzyme nor mops up the hormone after it forms; it holds one step of the process back, and everything downstream slows with it. That is what inhibitors do in any laboratory sentence: they act on the machinery, not the aftermath.

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

suppressant: A suppressant quiets an activity that is already raging — the cough, the appetite, the fever — without touching what drives it. An inhibitor reaches into the works: it binds a piece of the machinery so the process itself cannot run.

brake: A brake is the everyday, figurative check — rising interest rates put a brake on borrowing. An inhibitor is the laboratory's word, and it names a specific agent gripping a specific step of a process.

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

catalyst: a substance that speeds a reaction along

accelerant: anything that makes a process run faster and hotter

Where it sits · how completely the process is shut down

damper → inhibitor → neutralizer

damper vs. inhibitor: A damper is milder than an inhibitor: it takes the edge off a process that keeps on running, while an inhibitor grips the machinery and holds the process itself back.

neutralizer vs. inhibitor: A neutralizer goes further than an inhibitor: an inhibitor holds a process back and lets it resume when removed, while a neutralizer cancels the active agent outright, leaving nothing to restart.

Build the Word

The pieces

Prefix — in-: in, on — here turning the hold inward (Latin)

Root — hibit: to have, to hold (Latin habēre, in its combined form -hibēre)

Suffix — -or: the thing or agent that does it

Put it together: In- + habēre ('to have, to hold') fused into Latin inhibēre, 'to hold back,' and -or names the agent doing the holding. English keeps the same root busy everywhere — habit, habitat, exhibit, prohibit all carry it — but only here does the grip turn inward, closing on a process to keep it from running.

Use the root in a new word: habituate: The lab spends its first week habituating the new owls to the handlers' gloves.

Root Check

Word Choice

technical / science writing

Inhibitor is the science section's word: enzyme inhibitors, corrosion inhibitors, growth inhibitors — always a named agent gripping a named process. In everyday prose, reach for brake or check ('a brake on spending'). And keep the direction straight: an inhibitor holds a process back, while a catalyst hurries it along.
